chunks.text: III Detection Methodology III-A Progressive Heuristics The heuristic methods were developed in successive stages, beginning with simple intensity thresholding, image-specific adaptation and progressively incorporating biological knowledge about fluorescence colocalization and artifact rejection. This progression reflects increasing model complexity while maintaining interpretable decision rules and requiring no training . III-A 1 Intensity Thresholding We first investigated whether dead cells could be identified using fluorescence intensity alone. Three method variants operated on per-cell mean intensities measured within Cellpose masks. The first used a fixed percentile threshold, classifying cells in the top 1% (99th percentile) of both the green and red intensity distributions as dead. This represents the simplest assumption that apoptotic cells are consistently among the brightest cells in each image. The second estimated a threshold directly assuming a bimodal intensity distribution. A Gaussian kernel density estimate (KDE), with 512 grid points spanning the min to max intensity values, was computed from the per-cell intensities, and the first local minimum in the estimated density was used as the decision boundary. Local minima in the density curve were identified using relative minimum detection with an order parameter of 5 (requiring a dip between at least 5 data points). If no local minimum was detected, Otsu’s threshold was used instead. Cells above the identified thresholds in both the green and red channels were counted as dead. The third approach identified dead cells based on statistical deviations from the population mean in fluorescence intensity. For each image, we calculate z-scores as ( i ​ n ​ t ​ e ​ n ​ s ​ i ​ t ​ y − m ​ e ​ a ​ n ) / s ​ t ​ a ​ n ​ d ​ a ​ r ​ d ​ d ​ e ​ v ​ i ​ a ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n (intensity-mean)/standard\>deviation for both green and red channels, then classify cells with z > 2.0 z>2.0 in both channels as dead.

III-A 2 Adaptive Gap Split The previous method relied on fixing thresholds and implicitly assumed that every image contained dead cells. In practice, many images contained none. We therefore developed an adaptive method that identified the largest separation in sorted per-cell mean intensities as the natural boundary between live and dead populations while also allowing the absence of any boundary at all. The algorithm computed gaps between consecutive sorted intensity values, selected the maximum gap, and set its position at the midpoint between the two adjacent intensities. If this gap was less than 10% of the image’s intensity range (either green or red channel), the image was deemed to have no dead cells on account of an absence of bimodality. Similarly, the gap cannot sit down in the background noise. If the gap threshold did not sit in the 75th percentile (either green or red channel), the image was again assumed to have no dead cells. The rest of the images were deemed to contain dead cells, identified with intensities above the gap’s position. III-A 3 Colocalization-Aware Preprocessing Intensity alone is insufficient because apoptotic fluorescence must spatially follow the nuclear morphology. We therefore investigated two method variants that incorporated information from the blue nuclear channel before thresholding. The first calculated a blue-weighted intensity where a normalized nuclear/cellular intensity was multiplied pixelwise with the green and red channels before computing per-cell mean intensities, thereby emphasizing fluorescence originating from the nucleus. Cells exceeding the 99th percentile of the resulting scores in each of the green and red channel were classified as dead. The second replaced simple blue-weighting approach with computed Pearson correlations between blue and green/red pixel intensities within each Cellpose mask.

For each mask, we computed Pearson correlations between blue (nucleus) and green/red pixel values: r g , b = corr ⁡ ( G , B ) r_{g,b}=\mathrm{corr}(G,B) and r r , b = corr ⁡ ( R , B ) r_{r,b}=\mathrm{corr}(R,B) . Cells with positive correlations ( r > 0 r>0 ) were marked as dead if their mean green and mean red intensities exceeded their 99th percentiles among the positively correlated cells. III-A 4 Domain Expert-Informed Pipeline Although adaptive metrics reduce dependence on fixed thresholds, and colocalization ensures we only use relevant stain signals, the pipeline remained susceptible to noisy artifacts near cellular boundaries or bright/blotchy spots from debris or noise. Guided by domain knowledge, we built upon colocalization-aware preprocessing method through an iterative refinement process. First, we tried incorporating and seeing the affect of adding a coefficient of variation (CV) filter in the colocalization-aware preprocessing (Pearson) method: cells with CV = σ / μ > 1.0 \mathrm{CV}=\sigma/\mu>1.0 were excluded from the dead-cell prediction set, effectively removing cells with highly concentrated intensity distributions while retaining uniformly bright apoptotic nuclei. Similarly, we checked the effect of applying boundary erosion (3 pixels) to the segmentation masks before applying Pearson Correlation and CV filters, to hopefully reduce false positives arising from edge artifacts, ensuring that only robust intracellular signal contributed to intensity measurements. Finally, in order to be faithful to the domain scientist’s point-of-view where the red channel was used solely as a secondary confirmation marker, we implemented a sophisticated prediction scheme. Cells exceeding the 99th percentile in green intensity (after erosion, Pearson, and CV filtering) were classified as dead.

An additional set of cells in the 98 − - 99 percentile range in green were classified as dead only if they also passed the red channel’s 99th percentile threshold (calculated after erosion, Pearson, and CV filtering on the red channel). III-B Classification Detecting rare events such as a single dead cell among hundreds of healthy ones represents an extreme class imbalance classification problem. We employed both traditional and deep learning based classification approaches. III-B 1 Using Numerical Features We evaluated four traditional classifiers: Logistic Regression with balanced class weights and a maximum of 2000 iterations, Balanced Random Forest with 500 estimators using balanced_subsample weighting, XGBoost with a logloss objective and 500 estimators (no label encoder), and LightGBM with 500 estimators. Models were trained on a total of 27 features extracted from the three-channel cell masks and image patches as detailed in Table II . These consisted of per-channel statistical features - mean, median, maximum, and minimum intensity for each channel, and a Coefficient of Variation value for the cell mask. The 27 numerical features detailed in Table II were selected following preliminary feature-reduction trials. The candidate pool comprised over 60 features, including intermediate quartiles, standard deviations, and inter-quartile ranges computed across the cell mask, image patch, and global image scopes. Spatial features such as cell shape and area, were intentionally excluded from this feature set under the premise that complex geometric attributes are more robustly modeled by deep learning architectures. Furthermore, domain experts advised that morphological dimensions do not correlate with apoptotic indicators in this target distribution. All features were standardized using StandardScaler prior to training. Decision thresholds were selected using group-aware five-fold cross-validation to maximize the macro-F1 score.

Training used 80/20 train/test splits (the test set contained 53 dead cells) on the dataset shown in Table I (h-k). Pixel values were first scaled to [0, 1] by dividing by 65535 as mentioned before, then normalized using ImageNet statistics ( μ = [ 0.485 , 0.456 , 0.406 ] \mu=[0.485,0.456,0.406] , σ = [ 0.229 , 0.224 , 0.225 ] \sigma=[0.229,0.224,0.225] ) which is important for pretrained models [ 22 ] . Models used weighted binary cross-entropy loss with positive class weight computed as the inverse of dead-cell prevalence in the training set, AdamW optimization with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , mixed-precision training on GPU with channel-last memory format when available [ 23 ] . Decision thresholds were selected via group-aware five-fold cross-validation on the training set to maximize macro-F1 score. Training used 80/20 train/test splits (the test set contained 53 dead cells) on the dataset shown in Table I (h-k). Training was done purely on image patches: No mask information or numerical features were used . III-C Anomaly Detection As a complementary direction, we considered anomaly detection models trained only on live cells . The underlying assumption was that dead cells form a minority and deviate from the appearance of healthy cells in either numerical feature or image space. In this setting, high reconstruction error or outlier scores are interpreted as evidence of abnormality.

We used both numerical and image features for several anomaly detection models trained exclusively on live cells, using identical datasets and splits that were used with the classification models. III-C 1 Using Numerical Features We evaluated ( Isolation Forest with 500 estimators and contamination matching training dead-cell prevalence (approximately 0.37%), PCA reconstruction with explained variance of 95%, One-Class SVM with RBF kernel and ν \nu (the upper bound on the fraction of training errors) set to the training dead-cell fraction (0.0037). All features were standardized using StandardScaler . III-C 2 Using Image Features We trained a Convolutional Autoencoder with three convolutional encoder layers and stride-2 convolutions followed by transposed decoder and a Deep SVDD model with 64-dimensional latent representation. Both models were trained for 20 epochs using AdamW optimization (learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} ) with mixed-precision training on GPU when available. Anomaly scores corresponded to reconstruction error (squared difference between input and output) for the autoencoder, and squared Euclidean distance from the learned center in latent space for Deep SVDD. Thresholds were set at the 99.63 percentile of live cell anomaly scores (corresponding to the 0.37% dead-cell prevalence). Deep learning and traditional classification using numerical features achieved the strongest overall performance. ResNet-18 trained on 64-pixel unpadded patches obtained the highest dead-cell F1-score (0.617) and macro-F1 (0.808). Traditional classification methods were highly competitive, with XGBoost reaching an F1-score of 0.608. Heuristic methods showed moderate success, while anomaly detection models consistently underperformed the supervised methods. These findings highlight the trade-offs between representation capacity, reliance on explicitly labeled examples, and domain interpretability. IV-A Heuristics Among the heuristic methods, Intensity Thresholding using the 99th percentile achieved the highest performance, reaching an F1-score of 0.437 and macro-F1 of 0.717. Distribution-based thresholding methods performed worse, indicating that the fluorescence distributions frequently lack a well-defined separating minimum.

This was further made clear by the next method that was tried: The Adaptive Gap Split relaxed the assumption that every image contains dead cells, achieving a decent F1 of 0.427, but it could neither surpass the simple fixed percentile thresholding nor was successful at correctly identifying images that contained zero dead cells. For the reported gap size and position settings, the Adaptive Gap Split could only correctly identify 73 out of 125 images that contained no dead cells. These results strongly indicate that the dataset lacks true bimodality. Figure 2 shows example images to help the reader visualize what the image channels, ground truth annotations, segmentation masks, and model predictions look like for true and false positives and negatives. Introducing colocalization information through Pearson correlation or nuclear-normalized intensity did not yield noticeable improvements or degradation in the performance, suggesting that simple measures of spatial agreement remain insufficient to fully separate genuine apoptotic staining from bright imaging artifacts. Similarly, incorporating a coefficient of variation filter and cell boundary erosion further could not improve the performance in this dataset, illustrating the severe trade-off between specificity and sensitivity when manually designing decision rules. However, given that the Domain Expert-Informed Pipeline did not significantly degrade the performance and that all heuristic parameters can be fine-tuned for a given dataset, we believe that this method should still be prescribed in semi-automated or human-in-the-loop systems, offering a transparent algorithm that machine-learning methods cannot match. IV-B Classification Among the classification models using numerical features, XGBoost achieved the highest performance with an F1-score of 0.608 using 64-pixel padded patches.

Balanced Random Forest also demonstrated strong predictive capability, reaching an F1 of 0.538 under the same patch configuration. Increasing the patch size from 32 to 64 pixels somewhat improved the performance. Classification using image features outperformed all other computational families. ResNet-18 trained on 64-pixel unpadded patches achieved the highest overall performance (F1 = 0.617, macro-F1 = 0.808), while EfficientNet-B0 also demonstrated top results in the remaining three metrics (PR-AUC, Precision, and Recall). 64-pixel crops performed much more strongly, indicating that surrounding spatial context, when learned directly from raw image data, contributes highly useful discriminative information for identifying rare apoptotic events. Figure 3 shows example images to help the reader visualize what the image channels, segmentation masks, and model predictions look like for true and false positives and negatives. IV-C Anomaly Detection Anomaly detection methods underperformed classification approaches. Among numerical feature-based models, PCA Reconstruction produced the strongest results with an F1 of 0.361 using 64-pixel unpadded patches. Image-based approaches, including convolutional autoencoders and Deep SVDD, failed to identify dead cells reliably or at all, yielding several zero or near-zero F1-scores. These findings suggest that apoptotic nuclei do not simply represent statistical outliers in either feature space or image space. Instead, they occupy a complex region that overlaps substantially with healthy populations, making anomaly detection highly difficult without explicit positive examples. V Discussion We systematically compared a spectrum of computational strategies, from interpretable heuristics to traditional and deep-learning based classification and anomaly detection, for a very challenging fluorescence microscopy classification problem.

Note that heuristic models need no training, numerical based models used no images (spatial information) in training, image based models used no mask or numerical features in training, and anomaly detection models were trained exclusively on numerical/image data belonging to live cells. Why is automated dead-cell detection difficult? Automated dead-cell detection represents a particularly challenging computer vision problem because multiple independent sources of uncertainty accumulate throughout the analysis pipeline. First, the quality of downstream classification is limited by segmentation accuracy. Missed or merged nuclei or imperfect boundaries directly affect every subsequent measurement (Figure 2 b, d). Second, fluorescence intensity alone is an unreliable indicator: In practice and in our data, fluorescence images contain non-nuclear background noise for the apoptotic marker as well (Figure 2 a). Because the fluorescent dyes strictly target the nuclei rather than the whole cell, apoptotic nuclei appear uniformly bright when dead; however, overall staining intensity varies considerably between images, and many acquisitions contain no dead cells at all. Bright fluorescence can also arise from debris or nonspecific staining, producing signals that resemble apoptotic events (Figure 2 a, c). Finally, the dataset presents an extreme class imbalance, with dead cells representing only approximately 0.37% of all segmented targets. Such imbalance severely limits the statistical power available for learning while making false positives highly costly. Heuristics versus supervised classification The progression observed across the heuristic methods provides an interesting perspective. Each successive heuristic attempted to encode additional biological knowledge by improving signal representation or rejecting artifacts. Although these refinements increased interpretability, they highlighted the difficulty of manually specifying all relevant decision rules.

Supervised classification, particularly deep learning (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0) and gradient boosting (XGBoost), effectively learned these complex relationships directly from the data. Rather than relying on explicit intensity thresholds, these models captured the spatial information in the images and gracefully modeled the uniformly bright nature of the target nuclei alongside the contextual information surrounding them. Practical implications Although fully automated detection of extremely rare events remains challenging, the presented pipeline is immediately applicable as a decision-support tool. Rather than replacing manual inspection, the best-performing models can prioritize a small subset of candidate cells for expert review, substantially reducing annotation effort during large-scale screening. This human-in-the-loop workflow accelerates dataset annotation, improves consistency, and facilitates the creation of larger labeled datasets. VI Conclusions This study presented a comprehensive evaluation of heuristic algorithms, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and anomaly detection methods for automated dead-cell detection in fluorescence microscopy. Using a highly imbalanced dataset containing over 65,000 segmented targets and only 243 annotated dead cells, we systematically compared the efficacy of each computational strategy. Classification using numerical features (traditional) and image features (deep-learning) achieved the highest performance, with ResNet-18 (F1 = 0.617) and XGBoost (F1 = 0.608) significantly outperforming manually designed heuristics and anomaly detection methods. While deterministic rules and isolation algorithms struggle to separate the uniformly bright apoptotic nuclei from overlapping fluorescence artifacts, supervised models successfully leverage surrounding spatial context to improve classification.

Ultimately, while fully autonomous detection remains challenging due to inherent staining variability and segmentation limits, these top-performing models provide an immediately viable human-in-the-loop solution. Automatically prioritizing candidate nuclei for expert review can drastically reduce manual effort, ensuring highly scalable and consistent analysis in biomedical imaging applications.
